text: Course 13's final lesson ran the real CTA panel-defense format against Meridian's architecture decisions -- a candidate presents, and a panel pushes back in real time. This capstone made a narrower set of decisions: not whether Meridian gets one instance, but how a Service Desk actually gets built, integrated, tested, and rolled out. The same format applies here, against an actual build instead of a diagram.

First challenge: why not integrate with Prairie View in real time instead of a scheduled pull? The honest answer starts with the constraint -- Prairie View's homegrown system has no webhook or event capability at all, only a read endpoint. A real-time integration wasn't a harder version of the chosen design; it was never available. An inline call would put every ticket submission behind a legacy system's uptime. The scheduled pull decouples the two, at the cost of a staleness window already named and accepted.

Second challenge: isn't three flows safer than one, if each hospital's needs diverge later? Three near-identical flows sound more flexible -- in practice, they're three places the same logic quietly drifts out of sync. One domain-aware flow is the only version that proves a Lakeshore request lands with a Lakeshore group every single time, not most of the time across three maintained copies that can silently disagree with each other.

Third: nobody got exactly what they asked for in the category model -- didn't requirements gathering fail? No -- it surfaced a genuine structural conflict honestly, and a real conflict like that doesn't have an everyone-wins answer. The two-layer compromise gave each side its real concern. Fourth: why pilot at the most capable site instead of the smallest? Because St. Catherine's staff are most likely to catch and precisely describe a real defect -- protecting Lakeshore and Prairie View, the two systems that can least afford a rocky first impression.

Every answer here is built from a real constraint, a real alternative, and a real cost accepted -- not a rehearsed line, because a real panel can tell the difference immediately. But a build that survives a panel's questions can still have a genuine gap nobody asked about yet. The next lesson simulates exactly that: a reviewing architect finds one real, specific weakness in this capstone's design, and walks through revising it.
